purpose: Limits electric current and divides voltage. Without resistors, components like LEDs would draw destructive currents and burn out instantly, and microcontroller input pins would float into erratic, phantom states.

whenToUse.why: LEDs have nearly zero internal resistance once they begin conducting. Connecting an LED directly between 5V and GND creates a short circuit that burns out the LED and can destroy the Arduino pin.

An unconnected digital pin acts like an antenna, picking up static electromagnetic noise and randomly toggling between HIGH and LOW. A 10kΩ resistor anchors the pin to a known state until the button is pressed.
whenToUse.recommended: 10 kΩ resistor (or use Arduino's internal INPUT_PULLUP)

whenToUse.scenario: Voltage Dividers for Analog Sensors (LDR, Thermistor, FSR)
whenToUse.why: Sensors like photoresistors and force sensors change their resistance, not voltage. Arduino analog pins can only read voltage (0–5V). Pairing the sensor with a fixed resistor converts changing resistance into readable voltage.
whenToUse.recommended: 10 kΩ fixed resistor paired with analog sensor

whenToUse.why: The I2C protocol uses open-drain pins that can only pull lines LOW. Without pull-up resistors to 5V or 3.3V, the communication line remains dead.
whenToUse.recommended: 4.7 kΩ pull-ups to VCC on both SDA and SCL

whenToUse.scenario: Base & Gate Protection for Transistors & MOSFETs
whenToUse.why: Limits inrush current into transistor bases and drains residual charges to ground so switches don't float during power-up.
whenToUse.recommended: 1 kΩ for BJT Base, 100Ω series + 10kΩ pull-down for MOSFET Gate

basics.title: What a resistor does
basics.text: It limits how much current can flow. Think of a narrow part in a water pipe: the narrower it is, the less water gets through.

basics.title: Ohm's law
basics.text: V = I × R. Voltage (volts) = current (amps) × resistance (ohms). If you know any two of them, you can work out the third.

basics.title: Picking an LED resistor
basics.text: R = (supply V − LED V) ÷ current. A red LED (2V) on 5V at 15 mA: (5 − 2) ÷ 0.015 = 200 Ω. Use the next common value up: 220 Ω.

basics.title: Power rating
basics.text: Kit resistors are ¼ watt. Power = V × I. Stay under half the rating: 5V across 100 Ω is 0.25 W, too much for a ¼ W resistor.

basics.title: No direction
basics.text: Resistors have no polarity. You can put them in either way round.

basics.title: Tolerance
basics.text: The last band tells how exact the value is. Gold = ±5%, so a 1 kΩ gold resistor can be anywhere from 950 Ω to 1050 Ω.

howToRead: Turn the resistor so the gold or silver band is on the right. On 5-band resistors the tolerance band is usually brown and set a little apart.
Read the first colours as digits: two digits on a 4-band resistor, three on a 5-band one.
The next band is the multiplier: it tells you how many zeros to add.
The last band is the tolerance (how exact the value is).
example: Yellow, Violet, Red, Gold = 4, 7, then 2 zeros = 4700 Ω = 4.7 kΩ, ±5%.
mnemonic: Better Be Right Or Your Great Big Venture Goes Wrong → Black, Brown, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Violet, Grey, White (0–9).
